claims.text: Systematically varying strain rate during tensile testing of FeNiCrMn will alter its mechanical response.
Varying tensile-test temperature will alter the mechanical response of FeNiCrMn.
The effects of strain rate and temperature occur through changes in the activation of deformation mechanisms.
Systematic variation of strain rate and temperature will produce a more favorable strength–ductility balance than standard testing conditions.
The starting FeNiCrMn material will have a uniform microstructure in an as-cast or homogenized state.
Controlled tensile tests can systematically vary strain rate and temperature.
Digital image correlation and microscopy can be used in situ to monitor deformation and microstructural evolution.
The proposed tests cover ambient to moderately elevated temperatures and a range of quasi-static strain rates.
Dislocation glide, twinning, or phase transformations may mediate the deformation response of FeNiCrMn.
Lower strain rates may promote deformation mechanisms that enhance ductility without significant strength loss.
Moderate temperature increases may promote deformation mechanisms that enhance ductility without significant strength loss.
Higher strain rates may increase the yield strength of FeNiCrMn.
Higher strain rates may reduce the ductility of FeNiCrMn.
Lower strain rate and moderately elevated temperature will improve ductility while maintaining strength relative to the baseline.
High-strain-rate conditions will produce higher yield strength but lower ductility than the baseline.
Prior mechanical studies of FeNiCrMn are limited.
The baseline is FeNiCrMn tested at room temperature and a standard quasi-static strain rate.
Extreme conditions outside the tested ranges might induce phase instability or localized failure.
Analogous studies on similar high-entropy alloys suggest the predicted strain-rate and temperature trends.
A lack of statistically significant changes in strength–ductility balance or absence of the expected microstructural mediators would falsify the hypothesis.
